Nataraja

Nataraja (Sanskrit: नटराज, IAST: Naṭarāja; Tamil: நடராஜர், Naṭarājar), also called Adalvallan (ஆடல்வல்லான், Ādalvallāṉ), is a depiction of Shiva, one of the main deities in Hinduism, as the divine cosmic dancer.
The pose and artwork are described in many Hindu texts such as the Tevaram and Thiruvasagam in Tamil and the Amshumadagama and Uttarakamika agama in Sanskrit and the Grantha texts.
Mahendravarman I in 6th century CE, which is known by Archeological Survey of India and Archeological Survey of Tamil Nadu as the oldest known Nataraja sculpture in India.
The stone reliefs at the Ellora Caves and the Badami Caves, by around the 6th century, are also among the oldest Nataraja sculptures in India.
According to Ananda Coomaraswamy, the name is related to Shiva's fame as the "Lord of Dancers" or "King of Actors".
Narteśvara stems from Nṛtta same as Nata which means "act, drama, dance" and Ishvara meaning "lord".
In Tamil, he is also called “Sabesan” (Tamil: சபேசன்) which splits as “Sabayil adum eesan” (Tamil: சபையில் ஆடும் ஈசன்) which means “The Lord who dances on the dais”.
Koothan(ta: கூத்தன், romanized: Kūththaṉ), Sabesan(ta: சபேசன், romanized: Sabēsaṉ), Ambalavanan (ta: அம்பலவாணன், romanized: Ambalavāṇaṉ) are other common names of Nataraja in Tamil texts.

The two most common forms of Shiva's dance are the Lasya (the gentle form of dance), associated with the creation of the world, and the Ananda Tandava (dance of bliss, the vigorous form of dance), associated with the destruction of weary worldviews—weary perspectives and lifestyles.
In essence, the Lasya and the Tandava are just two aspects of Shiva's nature; for he destroys in order to create, tearing down to build again.
His headdress often features a human skull (symbol of mortality), a crescent moon and a flower identified as that of the entheogenic plant Datura metel.
Four-armed figures are most typical, but ten-armed forms are also found from various places and periods, for example the Badami Caves and Ankor Wat.
The upper right hand holds a small drum shaped like an hourglass that is called a ḍamaru in Sanskrit.
A specific hand gesture (mudra) called ḍamaru-hasta (Sanskrit for "ḍamaru-hand") is used to hold the drum.
The three eyes alternatively symbolize an equilibrium of the three Guṇas: Sattva, Rajas and Tamas.
The slightly smiling face of Shiva represents his calmness despite being immersed in the contrasting forces of universe and his energetic dance.

One of the earliest known Nataraja artworks has been found in the archaeological site at Asanapat village in Odisha, which includes an inscription, and is dated to about the 6th century CE.
The Asanapat inscription also mentions a Shiva temple in the Saivacaryas kingdom.
Literary evidences shows that the bronze representation of Shiva's ananda-tandava appeared first in the Pallava period between 7th century and mid-9th centuries CE.
Around the 10th century, it emerged in Tamil Nadu in its mature and best-known expression in Chola bronzes, of various heights typically less than four feet.
Nataraja gained special significance and became a symbol of royalty in Tamil Nadu.
The dancing Shiva became a part of Chola era processions and religious festivals, a practice that continued thereafter.

In medieval era artworks and texts on dancing Shiva found in Nepal, Assam and Bengal, he is sometimes shown as dancing on his vahana (animal vehicle) Nandi, the bull; further, he is regionally called Narteshvara.
The depiction was informed of cosmic or metaphysical connotations is also argued on the basis of the testimony of the hymns of Tamil saints.
In 2004, a 2 meter statue of the dancing Shiva was unveiled at CERN, the European Center for Research in Particle Physics in Geneva.
The statue, symbolizing Shiva's cosmic dance of creation and destruction, was given to CERN by the Indian government to celebrate the research center's long association with India.

A special plaque next to the Shiva statue explains the metaphor of Shiva's cosmic dance with quotations from physicist Fritjof Capra: Hundreds of years ago, Indian artists created visual images of dancing Shivas in a beautiful series of bronzes.
Nataraja is celebrated in 108 poses of Bharatanatyam, with Sanskrit inscriptions from Natya Shastra, at the Nataraja temple in Chidambaram, Tamil Nadu, India.

Qutb Minar

The Qutb Minar, also spelled Qutub Minar and Qutab Minar, is a minaret and victory tower, built during the Delhi sultanate, and comprising the Qutb complex, a UNESCO World Heritage Site in Mehrauli, South Delhi, India.
Successive dynasties of the Delhi Sultanate continued the construction, and, in 1368, Firuz Shah Tughlaq rebuilt the top parts and added a cupola.
In general, minarets were slow to be used in India and are often detached from the main mosque where they exist.
The architecture of the minaret varies greatly from that of the typical style and design of the mosques constructed in the Middle East.
Historically, tower minarets were uncommon in South Asian-Islamic design until the 17th century, due to the slow adoption of the typical Middle Eastern style in India.
The style of these structures is influenced by the local architecture such as the Indic temples.
Like many mosques built in South Asia during this time period, the minaret was constructed by Hindu laborers and craftsmen but overseen by Muslim architects.
Since some of the craftsmen were Hindu and unfamiliar with the Quran, the inscriptions are a compilation of disarranged Quranic texts and other Arabic expressions.
Drawing references from their Ghurid homeland, Qutub-ud-Din Aibak and Shamsu’d-Din Iltutmish constructed a minar (minaret) at the south-eastern corner of the Quwwatu’l-Islam between 1199 and 1503.
Quwwat-ul-Islam Mosque, to the north-east of the Minar was built by Qutub-ud-Din Aibak in A.D.
Later, a lofty arched screen was erected, and the mosque was enlarged by Shams-ud- Din Itutmish (A.D.
The mosque complex is one of the earliest that survives in the Indian subcontinent.
The nearby pillared cupola called "Smith's Folly" is a remnant of the tower's 19th century restoration, which included an ill-advised attempt to add some more stories.
Major Robert Smith of the British Indian Army renovated the tower in 1828 and installed a pillared cupola over the fifth story, creating a sixth.
In 1505, an earthquake damaged the Qutb Minar; it was repaired by Sikander Lodi.
The cupola was taken down in 1848, under instructions from The Viscount Hardinge, the Governor General of India at the time.
The Ghurids, historically called the Shansabanis, were a clan of Tajik origin that hailed from Ghur, the mountainous region of modern-day western Afghanistan.
The Ghurids annexed Multan and Uch in the western Punjab in 1175–76, the northwestern regions around Peshawar in 1177, and the region of Sindh in 1185–86.
In 1193, Qutb al-Din Aibak conquered Delhi and implemented a Ghurid governorship in the province, and the congregational mosque, the Qutb Minar complex, was set up in 1193.

In the past, scholars believed that the complex was constructed to promote adoption of Islam amongst the Ghurids' new subjects as well as a symbol of the Ghurids' adherence to a socio-religious system.
After a lightning strike in 1369 damaged the then top story, the ruler at the time, Firuz Shah Tughlaq, replaced the damaged story and added one more.
Sher Shah Suri also added an entrance while he was ruling and the Mughal emperor Humayun was in exile.
The height of Qutb Minar is 72.5 meters, making it the tallest minaret in the world built of bricks.
The tower tapers, and has a 14.3 metres (47 feet) base diameter, reducing to 2.7 metres (9 feet) at the top of the peak.
At the foot of the tower is the Quwat Ul Islam Mosque.
The lowest story, also called the basement story, was completed during the lifetime of Ghiyath al-Din Muhammad, a sultan of the Ghurid dynasty.
There are also six horizontal bands with inscriptions inscribed in naskh, a style of Islamic calligraphy, on this story.
During reconstruction, Sultan Firuz Shah Tughlaq elected to reduce the size of the fourth story and then separated it into two stories.

On 18 May 2022, a former Regional Director of the Archaeological Survey of India, Dharamveer Sharma, claimed that Qutb Minar was built by Raja Vikramaditya in the fifth century to observe the changing position of the sun, without substantiating his assertion.
On 21 May 2022, the Secretary at the Ministry of Culture, Govind Mohan, decided to conduct excavation and iconography of idols found at Qutb Minar.
Excavation can be started in the south of the minaret at a distance of 15 meters from the mosque.
Before 1976, the general public was allowed access to the first floor of the minaret, via the internal staircase.

Sun Temple, Modhera
The Sun Temple of Modhera is a Hindu temple dedicated to the solar deity Surya, in the village of Modhera in Mehsana district, Gujarat, India.
The temple is situated on the bank of the river Pushpavati, and was constructed in the 11th century during the reign of Bhima I and Karna I of the Chaulukya dynasty.
The temple is no longer used for worship and is a protected monument maintained by the Archaeological Survey of India.
The temple complex has three components: Gūḍhamanḍapa, the shrine hall; Sabhamanḍapa, the assembly hall and Kunḍa, the reservoir.
Earlier, during 1024–1025, Mahmud of Ghazni had invaded Bhima's kingdom, and a force of around 20,000 soldiers had unsuccessfully tried to check his advance at Modhera.
Majumdar theorizes that the Sun Temple might have been built to commemorate this defense.
On a block in the western wall of the cella, there is an upside-down inscription "Vikram Samvat 1083" carelessly incised in Devnagari script which corresponds to 1026–1027 CE.
On stylistic grounds, it is known that the Kunda with its corner shrines was built earlier at the beginning of the 11th century.
The inscription is considered as the date of destruction by Ghazni instead of the construction.
Soon after Bhima had returned to power, the temple proper, the miniature and the niche shrines in the tank were built shortly after 1026 CE.
The temple is built on 23.6° latitude (approximately near Tropic of Cancer).
The temple is the Monument of National Importance and is maintained by the Archeological Survey of India.
The Sabhamandapa is not in continuation with Gudhamandapa but is placed little away as a separate structure.
The doorway is adorned with carved figures of a seated Surya (Sun God), Ganesha and Kubera accompanied by dancers and amorous couples in the surrounding panels.
Architecturally, the Garbhagriha is aligned in such a way that the first rays of the rising sun illuminate the image of Surya during the solar equinoxes.
The panels are adorned with depictions of various gods, with the figures of Surya prominently featured, reflecting the temple's dedication to him.
The figure of Surya is prominently carved in three niches of the shrine proper, as well as on each side of three windows in the outer wall of the Gudhamandapa.
In these depictions, Surya is shown standing, with two arms holding lotuses and being driven by seven horses.
Other figures along with Vishwakarma, Ganesha, and Saraswati include the eight Dikpals - Indra, Varuna, Agni, Yama, Nirrti, Kubera, Vayu and Ishan.
The Vimana featured horizontal geometrical and figurative bands that rose to form a shikhara resembling Mount Meru.
The central spire included several miniature shrines called Urushringa, whose form is inferred by the shrines located on the steps of the Kunda.
Base moldings The pitha is similar to the Gudhamandapa, but smaller in size, as two courses of fillets are omitted.
Wall moldings Above the Narathara, a band of figures depicting dancers and gods, called rajasena, is present.
The lower brackets feature makara which gives the structure its name Makara-Torana while the decorative elements give it name of chitra-torana.
Several figures of the panels are shown wearing West Asian attire including a belt and boots.
Other niches and corners are adorned with figures of Shiva and Vishnu in various forms, as well as depictions of Brahma, Nāga and goddesses.
The flat ceilings and lintels of sabhamandapa are carved with scenes from epics such as Ramayana.
The Kunda measures 176 feet from north to south and 120 feet from east to west.
Several miniature shrines and niches along the terrace walls contain images of deities including various Vaishnavite gods and goddesses such as Shitala.
